output.executive_summary: The brief reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods using July afternoon satellite measurements from 2023 to 2025 to examine tree canopy and land-surface temperature [S1][S2]. It found that each 10-percentage-point increase in canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density; impervious surface was the strongest single predictor [S1][S3]. The brief also reports higher July heat-related emergency calls in the hottest neighborhood quartile than in the coolest [S3]. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook, setting a 30% citywide canopy target by 2035, and estimates 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years [S4]. The authors caution that land-surface temperature differs from experienced air temperature, the study shows association rather than causation, and the 2024 imagery may not reflect later planting [S4].
output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026, reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. Its summary says each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief presents these findings as support for targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods [S1].

For methods, canopy cover was measured using 2024 aerial imagery and ranged from 6% to 41%. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, taken between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. The researchers used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors [S2].

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C. Their average temperatures differed by 6.4°C. The brief identifies share of impervious surface as the strongest single predictor of surface temperature and canopy cover as the second strongest. It also reports that July heat-related emergency calls were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile [S3].

The limitations section states that LST is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design demonstrates association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. The recommendations are to prioritize planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and set a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. The brief estimates that planting 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years [S4].

key_findings.text: Each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature, after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density.
Canopy cover ranged from 6% to 41% across the 48 neighborhoods; Eastgate averaged 41.2°C and Willow Park averaged 34.8°C, a difference of 6.4°C.
Share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, with canopy cover the second strongest.
July heat-related emergency calls were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile.

output.executive_summary: The Catalog Modernization Project is Amber: it remains on schedule for its planned November 17, 2026 go-live, but its forecast cost is $6,500 above the approved budget, mainly due to additional data-cleanup work [S1][S2]. Migration is 85% complete, and the quarter’s completed work included data mapping, a pilot migration, and usability testing of the new search interface [S1]. Staff training is in progress, and the steering committee approved extending the pilot to Eastgate and Millbrook [S2]. Key follow-up includes addressing duplicate-record and vendor staffing risks, circulating the revised training schedule, delivering a deduplication report, and confirming contingency funding [S3].
output.detailed_summary:
The report covers July 1 to September 30, 2026, and was prepared by Elena Vasquez, Project Manager, Harbor City Public Library; its report date is October 6, 2026. Overall status is Amber. The project is reported on schedule for go-live but over budget. Migration is 85% complete, with 412,000 of 485,000 catalog records transferred to the new platform provided by Larkspur Data Services LLC. The planned go-live date is November 17, 2026, when public access to the legacy catalog will end. During the quarter, data mapping was completed on July 24, 2026, the Central branch pilot migration was completed on August 28, 2026, and the new patron search interface passed usability testing with 18 volunteer patrons [S1].

The approved budget is $180,000, spending to date was $112,400 as of September 30, 2026, and the forecast at completion is $186,500—$6,500 over budget, mainly because of additional data-cleanup work. The milestones list data mapping and pilot migration as complete on their respective dates, staff training as in progress, and go-live as planned for November 17, 2026. On September 9, 2026, the steering committee approved extending the pilot to two additional branch libraries, Eastgate and Millbrook [S2].

The report identifies duplicate bibliographic records from the legacy system as a risk that may delay go-live. Tomas Lindqvist, Data Lead, owns this risk, with a deduplication script planned to run by October 20, 2026. A second risk is that Larkspur's lead migration engineer is leaving the vendor in November 2026; the project has requested a written staffing transition plan from Larkspur [S3].

The listed action items are for Elena Vasquez to circulate the revised staff training schedule by October 10, 2026; Tomas Lindqvist to deliver the deduplication report by October 20, 2026; and Finance to confirm contingency funding of $6,500 by October 31, 2026 [S3].

output.overview: Amendment No. 1 changes the monthly service fee, non-renewal notice period, and availability target, and adds a quarterly accessibility-reporting obligation. It states that all other Agreement terms remain unchanged and that the Amendment prevails if there is a conflict. [S5][S6][S7]

findings.description: Both documents identify Larkspur Data Services LLC as Provider and Harbor City Public Library as Client. The Amendment identifies the underlying Master Services Agreement as dated March 1, 2025. [S1][S5]
The Agreement sets the monthly service fee at $4,500.00. The Amendment changes it to $5,200.00 effective July 1, 2026, to cover hosting and support of the digital archive module. [S2][S5]
The Agreement requires written non-renewal notice at least sixty (60) days before the end of the then-current term. The Amendment changes that period to ninety (90) days. [S1][S5]

The Agreement requires monthly availability of at least 99.5%, excluding scheduled maintenance announced at least 48 hours in advance. The Amendment raises the target to 99.9%; it states that the Section 5.2 service-credit mechanism applies to the new target. [S3][S5][S6]

The Agreement provides credits for availability below its target: 5% of that month's service fee for each full 0.5 percentage point below target, up to 25% of the monthly fee. The Amendment says that this mechanism applies to the new 99.9% target, leaving the stated credit formula and cap in place while changing the target to which they apply. [S3][S5][S6]

The Agreement contains no stated quarterly accessibility-audit reporting obligation in the provisions provided. The Amendment adds Section 11, requiring Provider to deliver a quarterly accessibility audit report of the public catalog against WCAG 2.2 Level AA within fifteen (15) days after each calendar quarter ends. [S4][S6]

The Amendment states that, except as amended, all Agreement terms remain unchanged and in full force. Thus, the Agreement’s other stated provisions—including the implementation fee, payment terms, support response times, backup and data-protection obligations, termination provisions, and liability limit—are not changed by the Amendment as described. [S2][S3][S4][S7]

findings.topic: Written amendment requirement and amendment priority
findings.description: The Agreement says fee changes require a written amendment signed by both parties. Amendment No. 1 is signed by both parties and states that it prevails if it conflicts with the Agreement. [S2][S7]

output.limitations: The comparison is limited to the text provided. The Amendment’s stated effective date and revised terms are reported as written; no separate assessment is made of how they apply to particular renewal or billing dates.

output.overview: Both documents report the Catalog Modernization Project’s approved budget as $180,000 and forecast cost at completion as $186,500, a $6,500 overrun. They differ in the spending cutoff dates, treatment of the go-live schedule, and status of contingency funding. The finance memo also raises a question about staff training costs that the status report does not address.

findings.topic: Approved budget and forecast at completion
findings.description: Both documents state an approved budget of $180,000 and a forecast at completion of $186,500, implying a $6,500 overrun. [S2] [S4]

Spending to date is reported as $112,400 as of September 30, 2026 in the status report, versus $118,900 as of October 10, 2026 in the finance memo. The documents use different cutoff dates, so these figures are not directly comparable as same-date totals. [S2] [S4]

The status report says the planned go-live date remains November 17, 2026, while the finance memo’s schedule assumes go-live on December 1, 2026. The documents do not explain whether the finance date reflects a schedule change or is solely a financial planning assumption. [S1] [S5]

The status report lists Finance’s confirmation of $6,500 in contingency funding by October 31, 2026 as an action item. The later finance memo recommends that the steering committee approve $6,500 from the technology reserve, rather than reporting that the funding has already been approved. [S3] [S4]

findings.topic: Staff training costs in the forecast
findings.description: The finance memo asks whether staff training costs of $7,800 are included in the forecast at completion. The status report gives the forecast but does not state whether those training costs are included. [S2] [S5]
The finance memo identifies a final implementation installment of $9,000.00 payable to Larkspur in December 2026. The status report does not mention this installment. [S2] [S5]

output.limitations: The finance memo presents December 1, 2026 as a schedule assumption, not explicitly as an approved change to the project go-live date. The documents do not establish whether the staff training costs are included in the forecast or whether contingency funding was subsequently approved.
